findings.claim: Every lesson closes with a practice question typed '12 marks — Evaluate/Discuss' and mark-schemed '[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]'; nine of the ten exam tips coach students for '12-mark evaluations'.
findings.truth: The World Around Us paper is a 1-hour written paper of 60 marks (3 of them SPaG), with compulsory questions on all three themes and a separate Resource Booklet. Its question tariffs run from 1 to 8 marks. There is no 12-mark question, so the extended SPaG-assessed task is an 8-mark one. Retariffed to 8 marks plus 3 SPaG throughout.
findings.evidence: spec, Component 02 assessment block (30% of the GCSE, 1 hour, 60 marks, 3 SPaG marks) plus the 1-8 mark tariff range for this paper

findings.claim: 'Reduce sea-surface temperature by even one degree and coral algae begin to bleach, fish populations migrate, and entire reef ecosystems collapse.'
findings.truth: Mass bleaching is driven by warming, not cooling: about 1°C above the usual summer maximum causes corals to expel their zooxanthellae. Lesson 3 of this unit already teaches '1-2°C above normal', so Lesson 1 contradicted it and taught the mechanism backwards.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Coral bleaching (thermal 'hot spots' 1°C above the long-term monthly mean); L3 content of this unit

findings.claim: 'human activity has cleared 47% of original forest globally for farmland', with a flashcard answer 'About 47%'.
findings.truth: The world has about one third less forest than it had before the spread of agriculture, half of that loss in the last century. 47% is not a published forest-loss figure; it is close to the separate estimate of the fall in global tree numbers.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Deforestation ('one-third less than the forest cover before the expansion of agriculture'; '~30%' reduction through 2018), citing FAO

findings.claim: 'without limiting warming below 1.5°C, scientists project the loss of 70-90% of the reef by 2050', repeated in the mark scheme ('70-90% reef loss above 1.5°C warming') and a flashcard ('Above 1.5°C ... 70 to 90% reef loss by 2050').
findings.truth: The IPCC 1.5°C report projects that coral reefs decline by a further 70-90% AT 1.5°C, and by more than 99% at 2°C. The lesson made 70-90% the penalty for missing 1.5°C, which understates the risk and inverts the finding.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C ('Coral reefs are projected to decline by a further 70-90%' at 1.5°C; over 99% at 2°C)

findings.claim: 'The World Bank and UN now use a three-way classification rather than the old developed/developing binary'.
findings.truth: The AC / EDC / LIDC grouping is the IMF's, used in its World Economic Outlook. The World Bank instead sorts economies into four income bands by GNI per capita, and the UN does not use these three terms.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Developing country (IMF World Economic Outlook classifies advanced / emerging / developing; World Bank uses four income groups by Atlas-method GNI per capita)

findings.claim: 'Switzerland's HDI is 0.962, the world's highest. Niger sits at 0.394, the lowest.' Repeated in the exam tip, an 8-mark mark scheme, a knowledge check ('Switzerland has the world's highest HDI at 0.962') and a flashcard ('About 0.394, the world's lowest').
findings.truth: In the 2025 Human Development Report, Iceland leads on 0.972, Norway is second on 0.970 and Switzerland third on 0.969. Niger scores 0.419 and ranks 188th of 193 - low, but never the lowest in any recent edition. Values updated to the 2025 report (Brazil 0.786 as well) and both superlatives removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Human Development Index and List of countries by HDI (2025 report, 2023 data); Wikipedia, Niger (HDI 0.419, 188th)

findings.claim: 'an average baby born in Niger has a one-in-twelve chance of dying before its fifth birthday'.
findings.truth: Niger's under-five mortality rate is 114.8 deaths per 1,000 live births, which is about one in nine. One in twelve would be 83 per 1,000.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of countries by infant and under-five mortality rates (UN IGME, 2023: Niger 114.8 per 1,000, the world's highest)

findings.claim: 'Avoid the developed/developing binary - OCR examiners specifically reward AC/EDC/LIDC vocabulary.'
findings.truth: Invented examiner behaviour. The specification sets the AC / EDC / LIDC vocabulary; no published source says examiners give extra credit for it. Rewritten to point at the specification.
findings.evidence: spec section 2.2.1 (current patterns of ACs, EDCs and LIDCs); no examiner statement exists

findings.claim: 'The Democratic Republic of Congo holds around 70% of the world's cobalt'.
findings.truth: The DRC mines about 70% of world cobalt output but holds roughly half of world reserves, so 'holds' overstates the stock. The lesson's own flashcard already says 'produced'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the L5 flashcard; USGS cobalt production share

findings.claim: Nigeria is 'the most populous nation in Africa ... the continent's largest economy'.
findings.truth: Population is right, the economy claim is out of date. After the naira devaluations, IMF estimates put Nigeria third in Africa by nominal GDP (about $377bn) behind South Africa (about $480bn) and Egypt (about $430bn). Egypt is also larger on a purchasing-power basis.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of African countries by GDP (nominal), 2026 IMF estimates

findings.claim: 'Trade is unbalanced: high-value oil and gas exports against high-value manufactured imports'.
findings.truth: Describing both sides as high-value states no imbalance at all, and contradicts the lesson body, which teaches that Nigeria exports raw primary goods and imports high-value manufactures.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with L6 content ('exporting low-value primary goods and importing high-value manufactures')

findings.claim: During La Nina 'the Pacific east of South America cools'.
findings.truth: The Pacific lies west of South America; east of it is the Atlantic. La Nina cools the central and eastern Pacific off the Peruvian and Ecuadorean coast.
findings.evidence: world map; the lesson's own normal-year description ('the cool eastern Pacific, off Peru')

findings.claim: 'Wheat harvests fell by 36% in 2002 alone' - repeated in the exam tip, the 8-mark mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The fall was far bigger than 36%. Published Australian farm data put the value of the wheat crop at $6,356m in 2001-02 and $2,692m in 2002-03, a drop of about 58%; production fell from roughly 25 to 10 million tonnes. I could not find any published series in which 36% is the 2002 wheat figure, so I have not guessed what the number was meant to be. Options: (a) replace '36%' with 'by more than half' in all four places, or (b) leave and ask the original source. Recommendation: (a).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Agriculture in Australia (wheat production value by year, 2001-02 to 2005-06)
findings.ruling: Leave: unsourced replacement / textbook usage / quotation provenance (source queue).

findings.claim: Amazon medicines include 'curare (anaesthetic)'.
findings.truth: Curare is a muscle relaxant used alongside anaesthetics in surgery, not an anaesthetic itself. Too small to be worth an edit on its own.
findings.evidence: standard pharmacology

findings.claim: The Great Barrier Reef's five bleaching events were 'the most severe in 2024, affecting around 75% of the reef'.
findings.truth: Aerial surveys put the 2024 event at about 73% of reefs, while the 2022 event covered about 91% of reefs surveyed. 2024 is defensible as the most severe on coral mortality, not on extent. The 75% figure is close enough not to cost marks.
findings.evidence: AIMS / GBRMPA reef snapshots

findings.claim: 'India fifth-largest economy'.
findings.truth: India passed Japan into fourth place on IMF nominal GDP estimates in 2025. Accurate when written, now one place out.
findings.evidence: IMF World Economic Outlook 2025

findings.claim: In Nigeria, 'around half of workers are in farming'.
findings.truth: Modelled ILO estimates used by the World Bank put employment in agriculture at about 35% of total Nigerian employment; higher shares are quoted for people engaged in subsistence farming. The range in circulation is wide enough that I have not edited it.
findings.evidence: World Bank / ILO employment in agriculture series

findings.claim: Nigeria is taught throughout as an EDC.
findings.truth: The IMF, whose grouping the unit now credits after F5, lists Nigeria among low-income developing countries rather than emerging economies. The specification asks for 'one LIDC or EDC', so either label satisfies it and no mark is at risk, but Tom may want the unit to say which list it is following.
findings.evidence: spec section 2.2.3 ('Case study of one LIDC or EDC'); IMF World Economic Outlook country groupings

findings.claim: 'global average temperatures roughly 1.1°C higher than the 1850-1900 baseline'.
findings.truth: This is the IPCC AR6 figure for 2011-2020 and is still what most mark schemes carry, but single years have since passed 1.4°C. A fleet-wide currency question rather than an error.
findings.evidence: IPCC AR6; WMO State of the Global Climate

findings.claim: 'City reservoirs around Melbourne, Adelaide and Sydney dropped below 30% capacity'.
findings.truth: True for Melbourne (25.6% in 2009) but Sydney's storages bottomed near 34% in February 2007. The sentence over-reaches by naming Sydney.
findings.evidence: Melbourne Water and Sydney Water storage records

summary: Scope matches the three themes of the paper, the named rainforest, reef, country, city and drought case studies all satisfy the specification, and every knowledge-check answer key and match ordering in all ten lessons is correct. No lesson is listed as clean because the 12-mark practice question and the 12-mark exam-tip coaching run through all ten, on a paper whose tariffs stop at 8 marks. The substantive fixes are a backwards coral-bleaching mechanism, the IPCC 70-90% reef figure attached to the wrong side of 1.5°C, the AC/EDC/LIDC grouping credited to the World Bank and UN instead of the IMF, stale and superlative-inflated HDI values, Nigeria called Africa's largest economy, and a fabricated claim about what OCR examiners reward.
